title: Why the Most Powerful Tool for Teacher Growth is So Often Ignored
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele, building on a Peps McCrea video, asks why teacher rehearsal - watching a model, adapting it, and practising it repeatedly with colleague feedback - remains uncommon in CPD despite evidence that it outperforms discussion and reflection. He diagnoses 'rehearsal resistance' through three barriers: the privacy of teaching, which makes practising in front of peers feel exposing; the legacy of judgmental observation, which makes any watching feel like evaluation; and the belief that practice is only for novices, which experienced teachers can read as a slight on their expertise. His move is to treat these as legitimate professional obstacles rather than personal failings, and then to give leaders and coaches concrete tactics to reduce the friction. Those tactics are to keep reconnecting staff with why rehearsal matters, to establish explicit psychological-safety ground rules, and to shrink the change to one technique while leaders rehearse first. He concludes that schools which push through the initial awkwardness gain a shared language of practice, stronger alignment and camaraderie.
points: Rehearsal resistance is broken into three distinct causes - the privacy of the classroom, the legacy of evaluative observation, and the myth that practice is for beginners - each needing a different response.
Emanuele insists that mastery in any complex field requires continuous practice, drawing the parallel with musicians, tennis players and surgeons to answer experienced teachers' objections.
Psychological safety is made operational through non-negotiable ground rules: mistakes are acceptable, there are no consequences or ridicule, and what happens in the room stays there.
The most important lever is modelled vulnerability, with leaders rehearsing first and 'embarrassing yourself a bit' to show the space is safe.
quotes: Teacher rehearsal, or deliberate practice, is simple: we watch a model of an effective technique, adapt it for our own subjects and students, and then practice it multiple times with feedback from colleagues. Research shows this approach is significantly more powerful than methods like discussion and reflection. And yet, while many schools do it weekly many more don’t.

In schools, teaching can often be a really isolated act. We can go months, maybe even years, without a colleague watching us perform. Over time, this isolation can lead us to see teaching as a fundamentally private act.

This history has conditioned us to feel vulnerable and judged during any form of observation. Unless there is an exceptionally high degree of trust, the suggestion of being watched, even in a supportive rehearsal, can trigger anxiety and defensiveness.

For a long time, there has been a persistent perception that training was really only for those teachers at the start of their career or for colleagues who weren’t good enough. This leads many experienced, effective teachers to feel that a request to rehearse disrespects their expertise.

Leaders must go first. The most powerful way to build trust is for a leader to demonstrate vulnerability. By practicing first and even “embarrassing yourself a bit,” you show it’s a safe space and make others feel more comfortable and brave enough to try.

Schools that successfully push through the initial hump of rehearsal resistance gain more than just better teaching. They create a common language of practice, achieve stronger alignment between staff, and build a greater sense of camaraderie. These outcomes are more important than ever.
